newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian mkts rattled by creeping coup talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian mkts rattled by creeping coup talk.

text.p: Russian stocks and bonds fell on Thursday on talk of a "creeping coup" and analysts said political uncertainty would continue to rattle investors.

Most leading shares fell in nervous trade and Russian foreign debt prices slumped before regaining ground in a falling market after Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused national security chief Alexander Lebed of plotting a "creeping coup".
Lebed denied the charge.

"Right now, we are down two to three percent on the day. There is still a bit of nervousness about what exactly is going to happen on the political situation," said Brunswick Brokerage equities trader Martin Diggle.
Prices of Russian MinFin bonds eased about 1.5 points on the uncertainty and dealers said selling was mainly from abroad.

"What is going on is not good for Russia, especially ahead of the Eurobond issue. Everybody believes the country will be all right some day but at the moment the mood is more downward than upward," an International Moscow Bank dealer said.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin ordered the defence and interior ministers to ensure their troops stayed calm during this latest political row to unnnerve investors in Russia.

"The underlying sentiment is quite good but I think a lot of market participants have underestimated the potential political uncertainty in this country," said Dirk Damrau, head of research at Renaissance Capital.

Political infighting and speculation of a Kremlin power struggle have surfaced since President Boris Yeltsin, in a sanatorium preparing for heart surgery, won a July presidential election intended to put an end to uncertainty.

At the same time, there has been much good news. Russia won a better than expected credit rating for the debut Eurobond it is set to issue before the end of the year and an international offering by gas monopoly Gazprom is tempting investors.
Inflation is under control, the rouble is stable and, despite concern over budget revenues, the International Monetary Fund has praised the direction of Russian economic reform.
"The fundamentals are much better than they have been and much more comparable to a typical emerging market but political developments still could hold some surprises," Damrau said.
Damrau said equity investors had been more cautious than debt investors, most having been in Russia some time and grown accustomed to volatility.
Alexandre Babaian, chief investment strategist at CentreInvest Securities, said markets were "very nervous" but that leading shares had found support levels.
"There is a very big interest to buy on the worries, on the problems and history shows that whoever takes positions in problematic times has had huge returns." he said.

Babaian said non-political factors, such as the Gazprom issue, which he looked set to be oversubscribed, and the launch of an International Finance Corporation Russia index were positive for the market.
Christopher Granville, head of research at United City Bank said tensions existed in all governments and the Russian row, which he attributed to Lebed's style, should not be overblown.
"It doesn't amount to anything. Kulikov, in his bitterness and determination to get Lebed has overstretched himself.
"You have a constant surface instability caused by Lebed's style but over time the markets will discount this because it will be clear that these are storms in tea cups," he said.
Granville said significant new investment would not come in a rush but added: "There is gradually additional investment looking this way."
